newsitem.title: UK: British utilities count cost of excess profits tax.
newsitem.headline: British utilities count cost of excess profits tax.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government has said it will make a one-off tax on so-called excess profits of privatised utilities a central plank of its first budget on July 2.

The government, which won power in a landslide victory on May 1, has said the levy will "comfortably" fund a three billion pound ($4.9 billion) programme to cut unemployment but otherwise Chancellor Gordon Brown has kept details under wraps.
The market has largely factored in a levy of around five billion pounds ($8.2 billion) to give the government some flexibility, centred on electricity, gas and water companies, analysts said.
"Three to five billion pounds on electricity, gas and water. The market would be pretty comfortable with that," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Some weekend newspaper reports suggested the figure might have edged up towards seven billion pounds, however, with a few commentators eyeing 10 billion as a target figure, although these revisions could depend on how many companies are implicated.

Utility sector analysts are largely focusing on a figure around five billion pounds and expect a broad-base definition of companies which are liable to the tax followed by a formula to calculate specific liabilities which would narrow the levy's scope.

"We think the budget will give a wide definition for legal reasons, in order not to be open to accusations of prejudice. But the key will be in the detail of allocations from a yet to be determined formula," the analyst said.
Possible bases for calculation include turnover, relative returns or a measure of profits above a market average.
"The smaller the take, or the closer it is to five billion, the narrower the focus will be for its generation," the analyst added.

Companies were asked to submit comments on the tax to the paymaster general by the end of May and a Treasury spokesman said around a dozen had been in to see officials with a number of written submissions arriving as well.

Labour's target of "excess profits of privatised utilities" could cast a net wide enough to include British Telecommunications Plc (BT), the former British Gas utility Centrica and even Railtrack and BAA, as well as water and electricity companies.

There were even suggestions in newspapers over the weekend that Camelot Group Plc, a consortium of public companies awarded the licence to operate the national lottery, might come under the spotlight.

It incurred the wrath of the government last week by making 40 percent pay rises to executives while the sums raised for good causes sank and has now agreed to explore ways of making the company a non-profit organisation.

Electricity and water companies, meanwhile, have long been the focus of Labour and consumer lobby criticism over the chunky dividends and executive pay packets seen in the years since they were privatised by the previous Conservative government.

Water companies in particular have been under fire as they struggled to cope with a severe drought in 1995 and at a crisis summit two weeks ago the government vowed to make them plug leaks, which currently allow over 800 million gallons to seep out of pipes daily.
Several of these companies have taken the opportunity of annual results statements in the last two weeks to air their views on the tax publicly.

Electricity generator National Power said it should not be subject to the levy because it had not made excess profits and argued that because it was sold in tranches, the state had already reaped the benefit of share price rises and dividends in between sales.

Anglian Water said any proceeds from a levy on its business should be used in the area which it served, while multi-utility United Utilities wanted the government to treat it leniently because it had already given benefits to customers.
"Which of these arguments will be taken into account is anybody's guess. But it all becomes more of an issue if the tax is huge," said one sector analyst who asked not to be identified.
BT was also prompted to comment mid-May after Robinson was reported to have said he could not see how it would be exempt.
BT chairman Sir Iain Vallance said he would challenge the tax "if we are stung in a big way and if it can be challenged legally."
The government's lines of defence to ensure the tax is not challenged in the courts are wrapped up in the details which the market is awaiting.

On the one hand, it is expected to strive to make the definition of companies liable to the tax wide enough to squash any possible legal challenges while resistance from companies is likely to be higher the greater the size of the tax.

"Labour is looking to the city for a reaction. At the moment, the market seems to have factored in a tax of around five billion and if that is the amount, it would not be catastrophic," the sector analyst said.

"But in a sense it is a self-fulfilling prophecy. If rumours suggest the tax will be higher and the market adjusts, the government will feel it would be able to increase the levy without a drastic effect on shares," he added.
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
